architecture_decisions.title: Require merchant-scoped idempotent payment-intent creation
architecture_decisions.context: Merchant API calls cross unreliable client networks and may return an unknown result after provider acceptance. An automatically retried creation request can otherwise represent a second charge.
architecture_decisions.technical_problem: Define how retries identify a previously submitted intent without requiring the merchant to inspect gateway-specific behavior.

alternatives_considered.option: Allow every POST to create a new intent and require client-side reconciliation
Deduplicate by a fuzzy match on merchant, amount and timestamp
Use a merchant-scoped idempotency key bound to a normalized request fingerprint

architecture_decisions.selected_decision: The merchant-payments-v1 creation contract accepts a stable idempotency key. payment-api persists a key-to-intent association and returns the established intent for equivalent retries, while conflicting reuse returns a business conflict. gateway-router receives its own stable operation ID for safe retries.
architecture_decisions.rationale: A merchant-provided identifier is deterministic and can be tested across network loss. Fuzzy matching risks merging legitimate purchases, and relying entirely on clients would leave the payment boundary unsafe.
expected_consequences: Idempotency records need bounded retention and explicit conflict behavior
Status inquiries must distinguish pending outcomes from decline
Gateway timeouts remain operationally indeterminate until reconciled

architecture_decisions.title: Separate public-key verification from business authorization
architecture_decisions.context: Several product APIs need consistent verification of issuer, audience, expiry and signature when service identities rotate their signing keys.
architecture_decisions.technical_problem: Avoid embedding divergent token parsing and key refresh rules independently inside product code while preserving product-specific access checks.

alternatives_considered.option: Each product downloads and validates public keys independently
Every product calls identity-api for each request
Offer a shared token-validator with cached public JWKS key discovery

architecture_decisions.selected_decision: identity-api remains the issuer and public-jwks publisher. token-validator exposes a bounded verification decision using issuer/audience and an overlap-aware key cache; payment-api and checkout-service call the validator at documented protected boundaries.
architecture_decisions.rationale: A validator service standardizes cryptographic verification, avoids synchronous dependence on the issuer for every request and makes rotation rules reviewable in one interface.
expected_consequences: Validator availability and cache lifetime become shared concerns
A valid token does not authorize every merchant or report operation
Identity changes must be tested against current validator behavior

architecture_decisions.title: Publish payment and order lifecycle changes asynchronously
architecture_decisions.context: Reporting needs business state transitions from Pay and Commerce without adding synchronous analytics persistence to critical payment or checkout paths.
architecture_decisions.technical_problem: Make downstream consumers resilient to delays and replay while leaving the transactional stores as state authorities.

alternatives_considered.option: Polling payment and order databases across project boundaries
Writing directly to the analytics database during API requests
Publishing versioned domain events to an asynchronous transport

architecture_decisions.selected_decision: Pay publishes payment-lifecycle-events-v2 via NATS and Commerce publishes order-events-v1 via RabbitMQ. event-ingestor validates, deduplicates and stages messages; order notification work remains a separate Commerce delivery path.
architecture_decisions.rationale: Event publication isolates analytical throughput from payment authorization latency and avoids cross-domain database coupling. Existing product transports stay specific to their deployed workloads rather than imposing a wholesale messaging migration.
expected_consequences: Consumers tolerate at-least-once delivery, duplicates and reordering
Event schemas need major-version change rules and producer ownership
Analytics completeness is bounded by delayed or missing deliveries

architecture_decisions.title: Provide a common observability platform, keep product accountability
architecture_decisions.context: Product teams had disjoint instrumentation formats and service health indicators, making cross-service correlation difficult during routine operations.
architecture_decisions.technical_problem: Establish a common telemetry ingestion and dashboard vocabulary without shifting product incident accountability to the platform.

alternatives_considered.option: Separate monitoring stacks for each team
A single central team also owns every product's alerts
Shared OTLP, Prometheus and Grafana ingestion with product-owned signals

architecture_decisions.selected_decision: Platform Operations maintains observability-platform, while product services emit common service IDs, trace correlations and bounded metrics labels. The canonical service owner retains responsibility for meaning, threshold review and response to service signals.
architecture_decisions.rationale: Common transport reduces instrumentation translation and enables cross-boundary tracing; separating platform health from business-service ownership keeps diagnosis accountable.
expected_consequences: Instrumented edges must be explicitly documented and cannot be assumed for all fourteen services
Telemetry must omit secrets and customer payloads
Sampled traces do not establish complete execution history

architecture_decisions.title: Version interfaces independently of service release numbers
architecture_decisions.context: Multiple clients and message consumers move through deployment schedules independently. A patch release of a service need not change its public payload, while a field meaning may break an old consumer even when code compiles.
architecture_decisions.technical_problem: Make compatibility explicit and auditable across REST, gRPC and event boundaries.

alternatives_considered.option: Require coordinated same-day deployment of every dependent service
Tie exposed contract version to each service semver
Use stable contract identities with explicit major versions and effective dates

architecture_decisions.selected_decision: Maintain an Interface Registry that separates service version from interface version. Compatible optional fields may be additive within a major; changing required fields, amount units, enum semantics or idempotency guarantees requires a new major with a migration window.
architecture_decisions.rationale: Consumers can pin a published contract while providers deploy independently. Explicit versions support meaningful contract tests and historical interpretation of evidence.
expected_consequences: Providers must maintain overlapping versions during migration
Consumer inventory remains a source claim subject to verification
Unknown enum handling and event duplication need test coverage

architecture_decisions.title: Stage analytics events before publishing governed metrics models
architecture_decisions.context: Late and repeated payment/order events do not map directly to trustworthy financial and commerce reporting tables; source event time and ingestion time have different meaning.
architecture_decisions.technical_problem: Keep raw contract validation distinct from business metric transformation and expose model revisions to downstream reports.

alternatives_considered.option: Allow reporting-api to read events directly from NATS and RabbitMQ
Transform each delivery immediately into final report tables
Validate and stage, then run versioned incremental metric models

architecture_decisions.selected_decision: event-ingestor validates schema and writes staged-events-v1, preserving producer and ingestion timestamps. metrics-pipeline produces versioned metrics-model-v3 with reconciliation and late-event policies. reporting-api serves the published aggregate model and applies scoped policy decisions.
architecture_decisions.rationale: Separating acceptance, transformation and serving allows reprocessing of late data without making read APIs depend on transport delivery time or primary transactional databases.
expected_consequences: Staging adds storage and lifecycle management
Metric backfills require documented windows and reconciliation
Report responses need a data_as_of boundary rather than a claim of real-time completeness

architecture_decisions.title: Promote immutable artifacts through shared delivery infrastructure
architecture_decisions.context: Product teams need a repeatable release identity across staging and production, while environment-specific deployment policy must remain centrally governed.
architecture_decisions.technical_problem: Avoid situations where a rebuilt artifact changes between reviews and rollout or a product team bypasses environment controls.

alternatives_considered.option: Manual per-environment deployment instructions
Rebuild from the source branch at each environment
Build once and promote a content-addressed artifact through GitHub Actions, Argo CD and Kubernetes

architecture_decisions.selected_decision: Use deployment-platform to promote a reviewed artifact digest with an explicit environment target and status correlation. Product owners retain semantics and migration accountability; Platform Operations maintains the rollout mechanism.
architecture_decisions.rationale: An immutable artifact connects test evidence to the promoted binary, and a common control plane gives consistent environment gates without re-implementing them per service.
expected_consequences: A successful rollout must not be confused with correct service behavior
Incompatible schema migration can constrain rollback
Production details and approval records remain outside company-shared sources

architecture_decisions.title: Assign named service primaries and backups for cross-team changes
architecture_decisions.context: Cross-project dependencies and shared platforms complicate determining who reviews a change or keeps a service running when the primary engineer is unavailable.
architecture_decisions.technical_problem: Provide clear ownership while preserving the difference between product accountability, platform support and governance authority.

alternatives_considered.option: Infer ownership solely from team membership
Assign all cross-team dependencies to Platform Operations
Publish primary/backup service assignments and require affected owner reviews

architecture_decisions.selected_decision: Each canonical service has a primary and backup employee, anchored in owner assignments and a owning team; the two shared platforms have no owning product project. A change crosses to documented consumer owners for contract review, while admin-only governance actions remain distinct.
architecture_decisions.rationale: Named contacts make service-level review and escalation actionable, avoid treating shared platform operators as business approvers, and permit historical ownership reconstruction from dated assignments.
expected_consequences: Owners and assignments need revision discipline
Service coverage is not inferred from an individual's secondary team
Shared documentation grants read access only; it does not grant formal handoff authority
